issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may interfere with a factual finding when the first appellate court reached it by misplacing the burden of proof or disregarding a statutory presumption affecting the evidence.
material_facts: The defendant claimed ownership through adverse possession, while admitting the former owner’s ownership; the burden of proving adverse possession rested on him.
The land records for the relevant years favored the former owner and were presumed correct under the applicable land revenue law unless disproved.
The first appellate court assessed the defendant’s evidence before addressing the land records and then rejected those records largely on a misreading of a statement in a profits suit.
The High Court set aside the first appellate court’s finding, concluding that it had applied the evidence and burden of proof incorrectly.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to interfere in second appeal because the first appellate court’s approach involved a procedural defect that could have affected its decision on the merits. The defendant also failed to establish adverse possession on the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 100(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appellate court may interfere where a substantial procedural error or defect may have affected the merits. Sections 45(2) and 80(3) of the Central Provinces Land Revenue Act, 1917, made the relevant land records records of right and presumed their entries correct unless the contrary was shown. The burden of proving acquisition of ownership by adverse possession rested on the person asserting it. The Court relied on H. R. Ramachandran Ayyar v. Ramalingam Chettiar and Ladli Prasad Jaiswal v. Karnal Distillery Co. Ltd. for the proposition that a factual finding reached after wrongly placing the burden of proof may be challenged in second appeal.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from a decision of a lower appellate court.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_misplaced_burden: The lower appellate court placed the burden of proving a material fact on the wrong party.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_disregarded_presum: The lower appellate court rejected records presumed correct unless disproved without properly addressing that presumption.
predicates.procedural_error_may_affect_merits: The procedural error could have affected the decision on the merits.
predicates.second_appellate_court_may_interfere_wit: The second appellate court may set aside or interfere with the lower appellate court’s factual finding.

issues.definition: When a second appeal involves a lower appellate finding reached by misplacing the burden or disregarding records presumed correct, and that procedural error could affect the merits, the second appellate court may interfere with the finding.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may allow a pleading amendment based on a material event occurring after the suit began when the event gives rise to a fresh claim and allowing the amendment is just and can shorten the litigation.
material_facts: During the appeal, the person who had held a limited estate died.
The appellant claimed that he was the deceased person’s next reversioner and sought to amend his written statement to assert a right arising on her death.
The asserted claim could not have defeated the respondent’s claim during the deceased person’s lifetime, and the death gave rise to a fresh cause of action.
Allowing the amendment could shorten the litigation; the respondent was to be given reasonable time to reply and present any new plea.
issues.conclusion: The Court allowed the amendment, directed that the case return to the trial court for evidence and findings on the new plea and any reply, and permitted the respondent to raise a plea based on later-acquired rights.
issues.legal_principle: A suit is ordinarily tried on the cause of action existing when it was instituted, but a court, including an appellate court, may take notice of subsequent events and grant relief in changed circumstances where the original relief has become inappropriate, where noticing the change will shorten litigation, or where it is necessary to do complete justice. The Court relied on Rai Charan Mandal v. Biswanath Mandal.

rule.if: appeal_pending and material_event_after_suit_filing and event_created_fresh_claim and amendment_facilitates_justice_or_shortens_litigation

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal concerning the suit is pending when the application to amend is made.
predicates.material_event_after_suit_filing: A material event affecting the parties’ rights occurs after the suit is filed.
predicates.event_created_fresh_claim: The later event gives the party seeking amendment a claim that was not available before the event.
predicates.amendment_facilitates_justice_or_shorten: Allowing the amendment is just or is likely to shorten the litigation.
predicates.appellate_court_may_allow_pleading_amend: The appellate court may permit the party to amend a pleading to raise the claim arising from the later event.

issues.definition: If a material event occurs while an appeal is pending, creates a fresh claim, and allowing an amendment would serve justice or shorten litigation, the appellate court may permit the amendment.
